'''DeeAnn Marie Reeder''' (born May 30, 1969) is an American [[mammalogist]] who specializes in [[bats]] and their diseases.<ref>{{Cite web |title=DeeAnn Reeder - (2015-2018) Presidential Professor of Biology |url=https://www.bucknell.edu/fac-staff/deeann-reeder |access-date=2026-09-29 |website=www.bucknell.edu |language=en}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Reeder received her Bachelor of Arts in 1991 from the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and her Master of Science in 1997 from the [[University of California, Davis]]. In 2001, she earned her Ph.D. at UC Davis under the supervision of [[Sally Mendoza]], with a dissertation titled ''The biology of parenting in the monogamous titi monkey (''Callicebus moloch'')'', on various aspects of infant caregiving behavior in a captive colony of the [[coppery titi monkey]] (''Plecturocebus cupreus''<ref group=note>at the time considered conspecific with the [[red-bellied titi monkey]] ''P. moloch'', as the dusky titi monkey ''Callicebus moloch''</ref>).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.batcon.org/women-in-bat-conservation-deeann-m-reeder/ |title=Women in Bat Conservation: DeeAnn M. Reeder |publisher=Bat Conservation International |date=2015-03-30 |access-date=2021-12-19}}</ref>

After completing a postdoctoral fellowship under [[Thomas H. Kunz]] at [[Boston University]], she joined [[Bucknell University]] in [[Lewisburg, Pennsylvania]] as an assistant professor in 2005. She was promoted to full professor in 2014.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.wiareport.com/2014/09/bucknell-university-promotes-three-women-to-the-rank-of-full-professor/ |title=Bucknell University Promotes Three Women to the Rank of Full Professor |publisher=Women In Academia Report |date=2014-09-26 |access-date=2021-12-19}}</ref>

Her research focuses on disease ecology, behavior, physiology, and conservation in bats. She has studied the relationships between bat health, ecosystem health, and zoonotic disease risks in [[epauletted fruit bats]] in Central and East Africa. Reeder has also conducted extensive research on [[white-nose syndrome]] (WNS), a wildlife disease devastating North American bat populations. She holds a research appointment at the [[National Museum of Natural History]] of the [[Smithsonian Institution]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] In addition to her bat research, she is recognized internationally for studies of mammalian biodiversity, particularly in [[South Sudan]].<ref>[https://www.bucknell.edu/fac-staff/deeann-reeder DeeAnn Reeder], [[Bucknell University]]</ref>

In June 1993, together with [[Don E. Wilson]], Reeder co-edited the second edition of ''[[Mammal Species of the World]]'', which listed 26 orders and 4,629 species. The third edition followed in December 2005 in two volumes, covering 29 orders and 5,416 species. ''Mammal Species of the World'' became a standard reference work on mammals and is also available as an online database.<ref>[https://www.departments.bucknell.edu/biology/resources/msw3/ Mammal Species of the World Database]</ref>

In 2013, Reeder was part of the team that described the new monotypic genus ''Niumbaha'' for the [[pied bat]], originally described by [[Robert William Hayman]] in 1939 as a member of ''[[Glauconycteris]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Reeder |first1=DeeAnn M. |last2=Helgen |first2=Kristofer M. |last3=Vodzak |first3=Megan |last4=Lunde |first4=Darrin P. |last5=Ejotre |first5=Imran |title=A new genus for a rare African vespertilionid bat: insights from South Sudan |journal=ZooKeys |issue=285 |pages=89–115 |date=2013-04-05 |doi=10.3897/zookeys.285.4892 |doi-access=free |pmid=23805046 |pmc=3690973 |bibcode=2013ZooK..285...89R }}</ref>

In 2025, she published the book ''The Lives of Bats: A Natural History''.
